lessons.title: Calculating the Cost of Production per Kilogram
lessons.body:
To know if your dried fruit business is making money, you must first know exactly how much it costs to produce one kilogram of dried product. This is your cost of production per kilogram. Start by listing all your expenses for a batch. For example, you buy 10 kg of fresh mangoes at 1,000 shillings per kg, so raw materials cost 10,000 shillings. You also pay for electricity or firewood to run the dryer, say 2,000 shillings. Labour for peeling and slicing might be 3,000 shillings. Packaging materials like airtight bags cost 1,500 shillings. Add any transport to buy inputs or deliver to market, say 1,000 shillings. Total cost = 10,000 + 2,000 + 3,000 + 1,500 + 1,000 = 17,500 shillings.

Next, find out how many kilograms of dried mango you get. Fresh mangoes lose about 80% of their weight when dried. So 10 kg fresh gives about 2 kg dried. Now divide total cost by dried weight: 17,500 Ã· 2 = 8,750 shillings per kg. That is your cost of production per kilogram. If you sell below this, you make a loss. If you sell at 10,000 shillings per kg, your profit is 1,250 shillings per kg.

Always include all costs, even small ones like salt for pretreatment or cleaning supplies. If you use your own labour, put a fair wage for your time. Keep a notebook for each batch. Write date, fresh weight, dried weight, and every expense. After a few batches, you will know your average cost. This helps you set prices and spot when costs rise, like when mangoes are out of season. Remember, accurate costing is the foundation of a profitable business.

lessons.title: Setting Profitable Prices for Your Market
lessons.body:
Once you know your cost per kilogram, you can set a price that covers costs and gives you a profit. But you must also consider what customers are willing to pay. In many African markets, dried fruit is sold in small packets, like 100g or 250g. If your cost is 8,750 shillings per kg, then 100g costs 875 shillings. You might sell a 100g packet for 1,500 shillings. That gives a profit of 625 shillings per packet, or 6,250 shillings per kg. Check prices at local supermarkets, markets, and online. If others sell 100g for 1,200 shillings, you may need to lower your price or reduce costs. But never sell below cost.

Consider your target market. Health-conscious urban buyers may pay more for organic or unsulphured dried fruit. Tourists might buy fancy packaging. For bulk buyers like hotels or schools, you can offer a discount per kg, but ensure it still covers costs. A simple pricing formula: Price = Cost per kg + Desired profit margin. If you want a 30% margin, price = 8,750 + (0.30 Ã 8,750) = 11,375 shillings per kg. Round to 11,500 shillings.

Test your prices. Start with a small batch and see how fast it sells. If it sells out in a day, your price may be too low. If it sits for weeks, it may be too high. Adjust accordingly. Also, factor in seasonality: during mango season, costs are lower, so you can price competitively. Off-season, costs rise, so you may need to increase prices. Always explain your value: no additives, natural, locally made. That justifies a fair price. Keep records of what you charge and what customers say. Pricing is not permanent; review it every few months.

lessons.title: Keeping Simple Records of Sales and Expenses
lessons.body:
Record keeping is not paperwork for its own sakeâit is how you know if you are making a profit. Use a simple notebook or a free phone app like Excel or Google Sheets. Divide it into two main sections: sales and expenses. For every sale, write the date, quantity sold (e.g., 5 packets of 100g), unit price, and total amount received. For every expense, write the date, item (e.g., mangoes, electricity, packaging), and amount paid. Also note if it was cash or mobile money.

At the end of each week, add up total sales and total expenses. Subtract expenses from sales to get your profit or loss. For example, if you sold 50 packets at 1,500 shillings each, sales = 75,000 shillings. Expenses might be 40,000 shillings for mangoes, 5,000 for electricity, 7,500 for packaging, and 10,000 for labour. Total expenses = 62,500 shillings. Profit = 12,500 shillings. That is your weekly profit. Do this every week. You will quickly see patterns: which products sell best, which months are slow, and where you can cut costs.

Keep receipts for large purchases. If you use a phone app, take photos of receipts and attach them. Back up your data. If you use a notebook, keep it in a safe, dry place. At the end of each month, calculate your total profit. Compare it to previous months. If profit is dropping, check if expenses are rising or sales are falling. Records also help you get loans or grantsâlenders want to see your numbers. Start simple, but be consistent. Even a few lines a day will transform your business decisions.

lessons.title: Managing Cash Flow for a Small Drying Business
lessons.body:
Cash flow is the movement of money in and out of your business. Even if you are profitable on paper, you can run out of cash if you spend too much before sales come in. For a drying business, cash often goes out first: you buy fresh produce, pay for drying, packaging, and transport. Then you sell and get cash later. If you dry mangoes in December and sell in January, you need enough cash to cover December expenses. Plan ahead. Set aside money from previous sales to cover future production. For example, if you know you need 50,000 shillings for a batch, save 10,000 shillings each week for five weeks.

Keep a cash flow record. In your notebook, list all cash coming in (sales, loans) and going out (expenses, loan repayments). At the start of each week, note how much cash you have. After each transaction, update the balance. If you see the balance getting low, delay non-essential purchases or push for faster sales. Offer discounts for bulk buyers who pay immediately. Avoid borrowing for daily expenses; borrow only for investments that increase sales or reduce costs, like a better dryer.

Separate business and personal money. Use a separate mobile money account or cash box for the business. Pay yourself a fixed salary, say 20,000 shillings per month, instead of taking money randomly. That way, you always know your business cash position. During low seasons, you might need to reduce production or find alternative products like dried tomatoes or herbs. A simple cash flow forecast: for the next month, estimate sales and expenses. If you expect more expenses than sales, find ways to increase cash, like selling older stock at a discount. Good cash flow management keeps your business alive.

lessons.title: Understanding Profit Margins and Break-Even Point
lessons.body:
Profit margin is the percentage of each sale that is profit. It tells you how efficient your business is. To calculate profit margin, use this formula: Profit Margin = (Profit Ã· Sales) Ã 100. For example, if you sell 1 kg of dried mangoes for 11,500 shillings and your cost is 8,750 shillings, profit = 2,750 shillings. Profit margin = (2,750 Ã· 11,500) Ã 100 = 23.9%. That means for every 100 shillings in sales, you keep about 24 shillings as profit. A healthy margin for small food businesses is often 20-30%. If your margin is below 10%, you may need to raise prices or cut costs.

Break-even point is the number of units you must sell to cover all your costsâno profit, no loss. To find it, first calculate your total fixed costs (rent, equipment, salaries) per month. Suppose fixed costs are 50,000 shillings. Then calculate your contribution margin per unit: selling price minus variable cost per unit. If you sell 100g packets for 1,500 shillings and variable cost (mangoes, packaging, electricity) is 1,000 shillings, contribution margin = 500 shillings. Break-even point = Fixed Costs Ã· Contribution Margin = 50,000 Ã· 500 = 100 packets. So you must sell 100 packets per month just to cover costs. Every packet after that gives profit.

Knowing your break-even point helps you set sales targets. If you sell 150 packets, profit = (150 - 100) Ã 500 = 25,000 shillings. If you sell only 80 packets, you make a loss of 10,000 shillings. Use this to motivate yourself and your team. Also, if you reduce variable costs by buying mangoes in bulk, your contribution margin increases, lowering your break-even point. Review these numbers monthly. They are your business compass.

lessons.title: Using a Notebook or Phone App for Bookkeeping
lessons.body:
You do not need expensive software to keep good books. A simple notebook and pen work perfectly, as long as you are consistent. Choose a notebook with columns for date, description, money in, money out, and balance. At the top of each page, write the month and year. Every time you receive money, write it in the 'money in' column. Every time you spend, write it in 'money out'. After each entry, calculate the new balance. For example: start with 0. On 1st June, buy mangoes for 10,000 shillingsâbalance becomes -10,000. On 5th June, sell 20 packets for 30,000 shillingsâbalance becomes 20,000. This running balance shows your cash position at a glance.

If you have a smartphone, free apps like 'Money Manager' or 'Expense Manager' can make it easier. They allow you to take photos of receipts, set categories, and generate reports. Google Sheets is also free and works offline. Create a simple spreadsheet with columns: Date, Description, Category, Money In, Money Out, Balance. Use formulas to auto-calculate balance. You can also create charts to see trends. Whichever method you choose, back up your data. For notebooks, keep a photo of each page on your phone. For apps, enable cloud backup.

At the end of each month, summarize your records. Total money in, total money out, and final balance. Compare with previous months. This summary is your profit and loss statement. Use it to make decisions: if packaging costs are rising, find a cheaper supplier. If sales are growing, consider hiring help. Good bookkeeping also helps you when applying for a loan or grant. Lenders want to see clean records. Start todayâeven if you only write one sale and one expense. Consistency matters more than complexity. Your notebook or phone is your business's memory.

quiz.q: What is the cost of production per kilogram if total cost is 20,000 shillings and dried output is 2.5 kg?
quiz.explanation: Divide total cost by dried weight: 20,000 Ã· 2.5 = 8,000 shillings per kg.

quiz.q: Which of the following should NOT be included in calculating cost of production?
quiz.explanation: Personal entertainment is not a business expense and should not be included in production costs.

quiz.q: If fresh mangoes lose 80% weight during drying, how many kg of dried mangoes will you get from 20 kg fresh?
quiz.explanation: 80% weight loss means 20% remains: 20 kg Ã 0.20 = 4 kg dried.

quiz.q: Why is it important to include your own labour cost in production cost?
options: B) To know the true cost and value of your time
quiz.explanation: Including your labour gives a realistic cost and ensures you are not working for free.

quiz.q: If your cost per kg is 8,750 shillings and you want a 30% profit margin, what should be your selling price per kg?
quiz.explanation: Price = cost + (30% of cost) = 8,750 + 2,625 = 11,375 shillings.

quiz.q: What should you do if your dried fruit sells out very quickly at your current price?
options: B) Keep the price the same
quiz.explanation: Selling out quickly may indicate your price is too low; raising it could increase profit.

quiz.q: When setting prices, which of the following is NOT a key factor?
quiz.explanation: Your favourite colour is irrelevant to pricing decisions.

quiz.q: What is a good strategy for pricing during off-season when costs are higher?
options: B) Lower prices to attract customers
C) Increase prices to cover higher costs
quiz.explanation: Off-season costs are higher, so prices may need to increase to maintain profit.

quiz.q: If you sell 100g packets for 1,500 shillings and your cost per kg is 8,750 shillings, what is your profit per packet?
quiz.explanation: Cost per 100g = 875 shillings; profit = 1,500 - 875 = 625 shillings.

quiz.q: Why is it important to review your prices regularly?
options: B) To adapt to changing costs and market conditions
quiz.explanation: Regular review ensures prices remain profitable as costs and demand change.

quiz.q: In a record-keeping notebook, which column would you use to record money received from sales?
quiz.explanation: Money received is recorded in the 'Money In' column.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of keeping sales and expense records?
options: A) To fill up a notebook
B) To know if you are making a profit
C) To show off to friends
quiz.explanation: Records help you calculate profit and make informed business decisions.

quiz.q: If weekly sales are 75,000 shillings and total expenses are 62,500 shillings, what is the profit?
quiz.explanation: Profit = sales - expenses = 75,000 - 62,500 = 12,500 shillings.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a good practice for record keeping?
options: B) Keep receipts for large purchases
D) Remember everything in your head
quiz.explanation: Keeping receipts provides proof and helps accurate record keeping.

quiz.q: How often should you summarize your records to calculate profit?
options: C) Only when you feel like it
quiz.explanation: Regular summaries (weekly or monthly) help you track performance and make timely decisions.

quiz.q: What is cash flow?
options: A) The movement of money in and out of the business
B) The amount of profit made
quiz.explanation: Cash flow refers to the timing of cash inflows and outflows.

quiz.q: Why can a profitable business still run out of cash?
options: A) Because profit is not real
B) Because expenses are paid before sales are received
D) Because of too many customers
quiz.explanation: If you spend cash on production before receiving sales revenue, you may face a cash shortage.

quiz.q: What is a good way to manage cash flow during low season?
options: B) Save cash from high season
C) Borrow money for daily expenses
quiz.explanation: Saving cash during high season helps cover expenses during low season.

quiz.q: Why should you separate business and personal money?
options: B) To easily track business performance
quiz.explanation: Separating funds gives a clear picture of business cash position and profitability.

quiz.q: What is a cash flow forecast?
options: A) A guess of future cash inflows and outflows
B) A record of past sales
quiz.explanation: A cash flow forecast estimates future cash movements to help plan ahead.

quiz.q: If sales are 11,500 shillings and profit is 2,750 shillings, what is the profit margin?
What is break-even point?
options: A) The point where you make maximum profit
B) The point where total revenue equals total costs
C) The point where you start losing money
D) The point where you close the business
quiz.explanation: Break-even point is when sales cover all costs, resulting in zero profit or loss.

quiz.q: If fixed costs are 50,000 shillings and contribution margin per unit is 500 shillings, what is the break-even point in units?
quiz.explanation: Break-even = fixed costs Ã· contribution margin = 50,000 Ã· 500 = 100 units.

quiz.q: How can you lower your break-even point?
options: B) Reduce variable costs per unit
quiz.explanation: Reducing variable costs increases contribution margin, thus lowering break-even point.

quiz.q: If you sell 150 packets and break-even is 100 packets, what is your profit if contribution margin is 500 shillings?
quiz.explanation: Profit = (150 - 100) Ã 500 = 25,000 shillings.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a fixed cost for a small drying business?
quiz.explanation: Rent is a fixed cost as it does not change with production volume.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for bookkeeping if you don't have a smartphone?
quiz.explanation: A notebook and pen are accessible and effective for basic record keeping.

quiz.q: In a notebook, what does the 'balance' column show?
options: C) Running cash balance after each transaction
quiz.explanation: The balance column shows the current cash position after each entry.

quiz.q: Why is it important to back up your bookkeeping data?
options: A) To prevent loss of records
quiz.explanation: Backing up ensures you don't lose important financial records if your phone or notebook is lost.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a benefit of using a phone app for bookkeeping?
options: D) It works without a phone
quiz.explanation: Apps can automate calculations and generate reports, saving time.
